method: The fragment was written with no web search at all, resting on the Codex's library and region records and on the writer's memory; this recheck searched every fact beyond the Codex, the strongest first: the founders and owners with their years, the ranks, the sites and soils, the making and its months, the label words and every beat of the story.

Every source the fragment listed (the Codex's own library and two reference books, none opened) is replaced by pages a search returned, read: search; marked primary where the result came from the producer's own domain (coulee-de-serrant.com) or the Loire wine body (vinsdeloire.fr, InterLoire), or a producer's own technical sheet on a merchant's host. No Huet, Dagueneau, Rougeard or Mellot page of the house itself was reached.

A fact in two independent sources or one primary stands; a producer's own claim is hedged as its account; a fact in one secondary only, or nowhere, is softened or taken out and listed here. A writer's own site (The Wine Doctor, Wine with Seth, a critic's pages) was read as a lead and never cited. Facts the library states stand as the brief allows, except where a search contested them.

The rules were tried on every string: no living person named, no price, no score, nothing volatile (recent vintages, refused by the lint, became since the late 2010s), no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash; the questions for one right answer, plausible distractors and an explanation that teaches. The lint's notes left standing: the first vineyard of Domaine Huet and the first name of the Alphonse of the inn are facts with two sources, the First World War is a false alarm, and the most tightly wound and the most exotic are the library's own words for those wines.

tested: The founding of 1928 by a Paris bistro owner and his son Gaston, Le Haut-Lieu bought that year as the first vineyard (Wikipedia, the Rare Wine Co article, Decanter's Wine Legend): confirmed; the founder's health broken by the First World War confirmed, his gassing and his café found nowhere.

Gaston Huet's dates (born on 4 April 1910 at Plauzat by one profile, died in April 2002 aged 92 by the same profile, with Wikipedia and an obituary of April 2002 giving the year): confirmed, 1910 to 2002.
Five years a prisoner, in Oflag IV-D (the Rare Wine Co article, Dreyfus Ashby, a newspaper piece): confirmed; captured in 1940 and the tastings in the camp were found in no source and are cut.
Mayor of Vouvray from 1947 to 1989 (Decanter's profile and Wine Legend, Dreyfus Ashby; one account says 46 years, which the dates do not bear): confirmed.
The 1947 Haut-Lieu Moelleux as a wine of history (Decanter's Wine Legend, two pickings in October): confirmed.

Clos du Bourg in 1953 and Le Mont in 1957 (Dreyfus Ashby, Cream Wine; the Rare Wine Co article has Clos du Bourg farmed from 1953 and bought in 1963): Le Mont confirmed, Clos du Bourg now taken on in 1953.

The soils (the Rare Wine Co article: Le Haut-Lieu the richest, deep clay and limestone; its sheets: Le Mont green clay with stone, less clay and more stone than Le Haut-Lieu): confirmed and the wording moved to the sources.

The son in law: joined in 1971, ran the cellar from 1976, left in 2012 (several accounts and Decanter's report of his resignation); biodynamics in the late 1980s by two, a trial in 1988 by one, fully in 1990 by one: the record says the end of the 1980s.
The sale of 2003 to the Hwang family after Gaston's death (Wikipedia, the Rare Wine Co sheet): confirmed; a majority and an American buyer were not found and are cut.

The making: each vineyard made apart, whole bunches pressed uncrushed (Alliance Wine, Vinatis), fermentation as long as the juice's richness asks (the domaine's own sheet on a merchant's host); old barrels over winter and an April bottling in one importer sheet only, cut. The domain huet-echansonne.com returned nothing to a restricted search, and a fetch of an importer's sheet was refused by the network.

changed.was: Domaine Huet began in 1928, when a Paris café owner whose lungs had been damaged by gas in the First World War came to Vouvray for his health and bought Le Haut-Lieu, a house and vineyard on the plateau above the town. His son Gaston Huet (1910 to 2002) made the wine with him until 1940, when he was taken prisoner; he spent five years in a camp in Germany, where, as the story is told, he organised tastings and talks on wine for his fellow prisoners. He came home to make the 1947, a hot, rich year that is a Loire vintage of history, and served for decades as the town's mayor. The domaine added the walled Clos du Bourg in 1953 and Le Mont in 1957, and from then on bottled each of its three vineyards apart, dry, medium dry or sweet as the year allowed. His son in law, who made the wines for some four decades, turned the vineyards to biodynamic farming around 1990. In 2003 the family sold a majority of the domaine to an American buyer, who kept its ways. Le Haut-Lieu, the first of the three, is the plainest lesson in Chenin: one vineyard, one grape, and the year deciding whether the bottle is dry or sweet.
changed.now: Domaine Huet began in 1928, when a Paris bistro owner whose health had been broken in the First World War came to Vouvray with his son, Gaston Huet (1910 to 2002), and bought Le Haut-Lieu, the first of its vineyards. Taken prisoner in the Second World War, Gaston spent five years in Oflag IV-D, a prison camp in Germany. In 1947 he was elected mayor of Vouvray, an office he held until 1989, and that autumn he made a Haut-Lieu Moelleux that became a Loire wine of history. The domaine took on the walled Clos du Bourg in 1953 and bought Le Mont in 1957, and from then on made each of its three vineyards apart, dry, medium dry or sweet as the year allowed. His son in law joined in 1971, took charge of the cellar in 1976 and turned the vineyards to biodynamic farming at the end of the 1980s. Gaston Huet died in 2002, and in 2003 the domaine passed to the Hwang family, the son in law staying in the cellar until 2012. Le Haut-Lieu, the first of the three, is the plainest lesson in Chenin: one vineyard, one grape, and the year deciding whether the bottle is dry or sweet.
changed.why: The founder's broken health, not gas; Gaston with him from 1928; Oflag IV-D for five years, not a capture in 1940 nor tastings in the camp; mayor 1947 to 1989; Clos du Bourg taken on, since its purchase year is disputed; the son in law's 1971, 1976 and 2012 and biodynamics at the end of the 1980s; the Hwang family in 2003, not an American buyer of a majority.

changed.was: Cistercian monks planted the slope in 1130, on dark schist above the north bank of the Loire near Angers, and the vineyard has kept its walls and its single shape for close to nine centuries. In the twentieth century the writer Curnonsky (1872 to 1956), the prince of French gastronomes, counted its wine among the five great white wines of France. In 1962 the Joly family bought the estate, with the neighbouring vines of the Roche aux Moines. The founder's son took charge in the late 1970s after a career in banking and, having read the lectures on farming that Rudolf Steiner (1861 to 1925) gave in 1924, turned the vineyard to biodynamics in the early 1980s, an early convert in France. He became the method's loudest voice, writing and speaking for it across the world, and the slope became a place of pilgrimage for growers. Because the whole of the appellation is held by one estate, Coulée de Serrant is a rare case in French law: a vineyard that is a named cru, an appellation and a monopole at once. On a list it is the wine to explain Savennières: dry Chenin of great power, with an argument about farming in every bottle.
changed.now: Cistercian monks planted the slope in 1130, as the estate tells it, on schist above the north bank of the Loire near Angers, and it has been under vine ever since. The writer Curnonsky (1872 to 1956), born in Angers and elected prince of gastronomes in 1927, counted its wine, by the estate's account, among the five great white wines of France. In 1962 a Paris surgeon bought the estate with the Clos de la Coulée de Serrant. His son came home in 1977 after six years as an investment banker in New York and London and, having read Rudolf Steiner (1861 to 1925), whose lectures of 1924 began biodynamic farming, farmed the Coulée biodynamically from 1981 and the whole estate from 1984, an early convert in France. He became a voice for the method, writing books on it that were published in several languages. Because one estate holds the whole appellation, Coulée de Serrant is one of very few French appellations that is also a monopole. On a list it is the wine to explain Savennières: dry Chenin of great power, with an argument about farming in every bottle.
changed.why: The estate's account hedged; Curnonsky dated and placed; the surgeon of 1962; the banker's return in 1977; Steiner dated; 1981 and 1984; the books; the monopole told as one of very few appellations held by one producer, as the library and the Loire wine body give it.

changed.was: Didier Dagueneau (1956 to 2008) came from a family of growers in the Pouilly hills, but before wine he raced motorcycles, and he kept a racer's appetite for risk all his life. In 1982 he set up on his own at Saint-Andelain with a few rows of vines. Pouilly-Fumé was then mostly a quick, light wine made in steel and sold young, and he set out to show what the place could give. He cut yields hard, ploughed, picked ripe, fermented in barrel and left the wine on its lees, and he had long, narrow casks made to his own design. His neighbours called him a rebel, and his wines divided them, but the flint parcels of Saint-Andelain gave Silex, the bottle that made his name, and beside it came Pur Sang and, from ungrafted vines, Astéroïde. He later planted vines in Jurançon, in the far south west, for a sweet wine, Les Jardins de Babylone. In 2008 he died when his light aircraft crashed, and his son, who had worked beside him, took the domaine on and kept its ways. Silex is the bottle that proves Sauvignon Blanc can age: a Loire white to set beside a grand cru Chablis, never a crisp glass for the terrace.
changed.now: Didier Dagueneau (1956 to 2008) was born at Saint-Andelain into a family of growers, but before wine he raced motorcycle sidecars and drove sled dogs. In 1982 he set up an estate of his own rather than join the family's. Pouilly-Fumé was then often a thin, grassy white, made in steel and bottled early, and he set out to show what the place could give. He cut yields hard, spoke out against neighbours who overcropped, and raised his wines in oak, a large share of it new at first, with long, narrow casks made to his own design. The flint parcels gave Silex, the bottle that made his name, and beside it came Pur Sang and Buisson Renard, and in the far south west a sweet Jurançon, Les Jardins de Babylone. On 17 September 2008 he died when his microlight crashed near Cognac, and his son took the domaine on. Since the late 2010s the domaine has bottled Silex as Vin de France, outside the appellation, though it comes from the same flint. Through the twentieth century, when most of Saumur-Champigny was a light red to drink young, the family kept slower ways: hand picking, low yields, long ageing in barrel and bottling without filtration. Two brothers of the family ran the estate for decades and gave its three reds their shape: Le Clos, the estate wine; Les Poyeux, the perfumed parcel on sandier soil; and Le Bourg, the old vines, raised in new oak where the others went to older wood. They sold little and spoke less, and their wines passed from hand to hand among sommeliers and collectors before they ever reached a wine list. One of the brothers died in 2015, and in 2017 the family sold the estate to new owners, a family that had bought Château Montrose in Saint-Estèphe in 2006. Biodynamic and organic certification (one merchant, the library): kept without a year, which no source gave. A search restricted to the family's own domain returned nothing.

Génération XIX named for the nineteenth generation; Edmond from vines of forty to eighty years and more (iDealwine, merchants): the story's Edmond named for the nineteenth generation was wrong and is corrected.
The pick: merchants call La Moussière the family's flagship vineyard; the library calls Edmond the white flagship: kept, with the alternative for the integrator.

The rules: the heads of the family of these years, father and son, and the son's wife are not named outside the house's own name; no price, no score, nothing volatile (the thirty hectares in the results not carried), British, no dash; the questions sound.

By family custom the head of each generation came to be called Alphonse, so that the name on the label has passed from father to son for well over a century. Through the late twentieth century, when most Sancerre was made quickly in steel to be drunk young, the family turned towards lower yields and longer ageing, and the generation that took charge at the turn of this century farmed La Moussière biodynamically and worked part of its white in oak. Beside it the family bottles an old vine white, Cuvée Edmond, a selection named for its nineteenth generation, and Pinot Noir from single parcels, which shows Sancerre as a red appellation too.
